reports.text:
Subject: Misuse of road resurfacing funds in the Public Works Department

I am an employee of the city's Public Works Department and I am filing this report because I no longer believe the problem can be fixed internally. I have tried to raise it twice through my chain of command without any result.

Background. Each year the department receives a state grant for road resurfacing. The grant requires that the money be spent on streets rated 'poor' or 'failing' in the pavement condition survey. Since the start of this fiscal year, the deputy director of operations, Gerald Fairweather, has been directing crews to resurface streets that were rated 'good' in the survey. Almost all of these streets are in the neighborhood where he and two city council members live. At the same time, at least fourteen streets rated 'failing' were moved to next year's list. Residents on those streets who called to complain about potholes were told the repairs were already scheduled, which was not true.

How I know. I am the only GIS analyst in the department, and I maintain the pavement condition map that the grant reports are generated from. In the spring, I was asked by Mr. Fairweather's assistant, Lorraine Batts, to change the ratings for nine street segments from 'good' to 'poor' in the map before the mid-year report went to the state. I refused and documented the request in an email to my supervisor. Two weeks later I noticed that the ratings had been changed anyway, using a shared administrator account that only the deputy director's office uses.

I also work the Tuesday-to-Saturday schedule, so on Saturdays I am usually the only person in the office on the second floor annex. On three Saturdays this summer I watched Mr. Fairweather come in, use the shared terminal by the plotter, and leave within twenty minutes. The map audit history shows rating edits at exactly those times.

Financial impact. Based on the work orders, roughly $1.3 million of grant money has been spent on streets that did not qualify. The contractor on most of these jobs is Ridgeline Paving, which was not the lowest bidder on any of them. The work orders were approved by Mr. Fairweather alone, even though the purchasing policy requires a second signature above $50,000. Two change orders on these jobs were also raised after the work was finished, adding about $180,000 that is not explained anywhere in the project files.

What I have kept. I have exported the audit history of the pavement map, a copy of the original survey ratings, and the email I sent refusing the change. I have not shared these with anyone outside the department.

Why I am worried. I was hired as part of the 2019 cohort of the city's veterans hiring program, and I am the only person in my unit who came in that way, so I am easy to single out. After my second complaint, my performance review was moved up by four months and my remote work day was cancelled. I believe this was retaliation, and I am afraid that if this report is traced back to me I will lose my job.

I ask that this report be treated confidentially and that the investigation start with the map audit history and the purchasing records, which do not depend on my testimony.

I'm an adjuster in the property claims department, which has well over a hundred adjusters across several regional offices, and I review these files every day. Based on the monthly dashboards, roughly 1,200 claims were denied this way in the first half of the year. Adjusters who approve too many claims are placed on performance plans. The guidance was later removed from the shared drive, but copies exist in the inboxes of the adjusters who received it.

One family whose basement flooded after a pipe burst was denied twice and was only paid after their lawyer sent a demand letter. The denial letters use the same template language regardless of the facts of the claim, and the template came out of the director's office. Adjusters have asked in team meetings whether this is legal, and the answer has always been that the workflow was approved by senior leadership. reports.text:
I've been going back and forth for weeks about whether to send this, so I'm just going to write everything down and let you decide what to do with it.

I'm a dispatcher at a regional trucking company that hauls refrigerated freight, mostly produce and dairy, for grocery distribution centers. There are only two of us on dispatch and I cover the overnight desk alone from Sunday through Wednesday, so anything that happens between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. goes through me. That's how I found out about this.

The operations manager, Wade Hollister, has been telling drivers to run their electronic logging devices in a way that hides how long they are actually driving. He has them log off-duty time while they are waiting at the shipper, then drive straight through without the required break, and he edits the logs afterwards under the carrier admin account. Drivers who complain get the worst loads or get taken off the schedule for a week. I have heard him say on speakerphone that if the logs look clean, the insurance doesn't care.

It's not just a paperwork problem. Two months ago one of our drivers, a guy named Felipe Ortega, had been driving close to 16 hours when he rear-ended a car at a toll plaza. Nobody was killed, thank God, but the woman in the car was hurt badly. After the accident, Wade had the logs for that trip edited to show a ten-hour break that never happened. I know because I was the one on the phone with Felipe for most of that night trying to keep him awake, and the original log was on my screen before it changed.

There is also the reefer temperature issue. When a trailer's refrigeration unit fails on the road, the temperature logs are supposed to be sent to the customer and the load rejected. Wade has told the drivers to unplug the temperature recorders when that happens and plug them back in before delivery, so the gap looks like a sensor glitch. I've seen at least six loads of dairy delivered this way since the summer. The customers are grocery chains and that milk goes on shelves.

I keep a notebook at my desk because my memory isn't great since my concussion last year, and I wrote down the truck numbers, the trips and the times whenever something like this happened. I also took pictures of the log screens on my phone, before and after the edits. I know that probably wasn't allowed, but I didn't know what else to do.

I'm also scared because I'm the only one at the company who speaks Punjabi with the owner-operators, so a lot of the drivers come to me when they have problems, and Wade knows that. If he figures out that someone reported the log edits, he will think it was me or one of the drivers I talk to.

What I'm asking is that someone checks the ELD edit history for the carrier admin account, especially for the toll plaza accident trip, and the temperature recorder data for the dairy loads. I'm not asking for anything for myself. I just don't want somebody to die because a manager wanted to keep the trucks moving.

Sorry this is so long. I'm 58 and I don't know how easy it would be for me to find another job if this goes wrong, so I didn't know how to make it shorter without leaving things out.
